picked.t: Vingroup, controlled by Southeast Asia’s richest billionaire, orders 200 driverless metro trains from Alstom for Hanoi
picked.body: Under the deal signed Tuesday, Alstom will produce the first 83 trainsets at its factory in France before transferring technology and supplying key components for Vingroup to assemble the remaining 117 in Vietnam, according to the Vietnamese conglomerate controlled by billionaire Pham Nhat Vuong. Each train will consist of five aluminum-alloy cars, a design intended to reduce axle loads, lower energy consumption and minimize wear on the tracks. The trains will operate at GoA4, the highest grade of automation, allowing them to run without onboard drivers. Alstom, founded in 1928, is one of the world’s major manufacturers of trains, metro systems and locomotives, while also providing signaling and other railway technologies. The French company has supplied rolling stock and rail systems for major projects worldwide, including across Asia. It has operated in Vietnam for more than three decades. Its previous projects include signaling systems for the Hanoi-Vinh railway and Ninh Binh station, as well as 10 trains for Hanoi Metro Line 3, which runs between Nhon and Hanoi Railway Station. Vingroup is constructing the Hanoi metro through its subsidiary Vinhomes. The five lines have a combined length of 303.5 kilometers, linking the downtown area with destinations including Noi Bai International Airport, the Hoa Lac tech hub and the outskirt district of Dong Anh. VinSpeed, another Vingroup subsidiary, is developing Vietnam’s first two high-speed rail projects: the 54-kilometer Ben Thanh–Can Gio line in HCMC and the 120-kilometer Hanoi–Quang Ninh line. For these two, it has signed a contract worth 1 billion euros ($1.15 billion) with Siemens Mobility. Under the agreement, the German company will supply 10 trains and communications and electrification systems.

picked.t: Vietnamese trainees in Germany fight to move beyond ‘cheap labor’ image
picked.body: When Nguyen Van Bau arrived in Germany at 19 to begin vocational training at a hotel in Bavaria, he expected to learn the hospitality business. Instead, he found himself delivering bread for his boss and doing manual work such as clearing broken tiles from holiday apartments during the pandemic. "I felt like cheap labor," Bau says. Thu Trang, 23, had a similarly difficult start at a hospital in Leipzig. She says some colleagues gave her tasks outside her job description, refused to guide her and at times blocked her opportunities to learn. "Seeing that I was a foreigner, many colleagues dumped tasks outside the job description on me," she says. "When no one was around, they glared at me, bullied me, and blocked my learning opportunities." Bau and Trang are among more than 16,000 Vietnamese pursuing vocational training in Germany, according to the country’s 2024 Migration Report. For many, the biggest challenges go beyond tuition or living costs. Limited German, unfamiliarity with labor rights and difficulty adapting to a less hierarchical workplace culture can leave trainees vulnerable to exploitation or exclusion. Bau’s family spent €7,500 (US$8,400) on agency fees in 2019 and another €11,300 on language courses, housing and financial requirements. "My parents said it was an advance on my inheritance," he says. "With such a huge sum invested, failure meant there was no way back." Although vocational trainees are supposed to receive professional instruction, Bau says he was instead assigned manual work for less than €5 an hour, around half the minimum wage at the time, while being routinely scolded and belittled. After others warned him that he was being exploited, he began studying German labor law. With support from a hospitality workers’ union, he sued his former employer over excessive overtime during peak periods and won. In 2022, he moved to another hotel where he received structured training. A year later, he graduated with top marks, was promoted to shift supervisor and was earning three times his previous salary. "The biggest change wasn’t the salary, but my standing at work," he says. "I am no longer a passive placeholder." Trang took a different route. Before choosing an agency, she first selected her school and later joined a state-supported program costing about €4,000. She began nursing training at Leipzig University Hospital in June 2024 and was the only Vietnamese student in her class. The program proved demanding. Half of the original 30 students dropped out after the first semester. Trang says fast speech, technical vocabulary and subjects such as medical ethics forced her to work much harder than local classmates. She began carrying a notebook everywhere, writing down unfamiliar medical terms and the names of equipment she encountered. Before lessons, she searched for materials in Vietnamese and then translated them into German to prepare herself. "You can’t just blindly stumble through the medical field," she says. As her language skills improved, so did her confidence. She began refusing tasks she considered unreasonable and says she learned that speaking up often led to greater respect from colleagues. "I learned that daring to speak up earns you respect in this environment," she says. Taking control In 2024, Bau and two colleagues founded a company that recruits young Vietnamese for vocational training in Germany without charging them agency fees. Instead, the company receives €5,000 from German employers for each successful recruit. Applicants are expected to hold at least a B1 German certificate, or A2 combined with strong communication and problem-solving skills. Bau says the company places more emphasis on practical ability and how candidates respond to real situations than on qualifications alone. Language remains one of the biggest weaknesses among Vietnamese trainees. Christopher Gnadt, a lecturer at the University of Vechta with more than a decade of experience recruiting and managing nursing-home staff, says two issues often put Vietnamese workers at a disadvantage: weak German and a tendency to remain too deferential. "German employers do not expect an employee who simply knows how to obey," he says. "Timidity and reluctance to ask questions are often perceived as lack of competence." Nguyen Thi Loan, a nurse in her 30s in North Rhine-Westphalia, says her own experience shows how much language can change a migrant worker’s position. Born into a low-income family in Hanoi’s Soc Son District, she won a place in an affordable vocational training program in Germany because of her strong academic record. Today, she works as a practical instructor at four elderly-care facilities and operates a support hotline for Vietnamese trainees. She also helps her husband recruit Vietnamese workers for German employers and runs an SOS service for trainees facing problems with study, work or integration. picked.t: BUV, Manchester Metropolitan expand partnership on work-integrated education
picked.body: The agreement was signed by Rick Bennett, Deputy Vice-Chancellor of BUV, and Jenny Watling, Pro Vice-Chancellor (International) at Manchester Metropolitan University, at the British Ambassador's Residence in Hanoi on Oct. 7, witnessed by Baroness Jacqui Smith of Malvern, U.K. Minister of State for Skills; Professor Sir Steve Smith, U.K. International Education Champion; and Iain Frew, British Ambassador to Vietnam. Expanding programs and industry links The partnership began with a memorandum of understanding in November 2024 covering student mobility, collaborative online international learning, articulation pathways into Manchester Metropolitan's Business School, and industry engagement. In 2025, Manchester Metropolitan became an awarding body partner for BUV. In September 2026, more than 200 students began five undergraduate and postgraduate programs awarded by Manchester Metropolitan in business, finance, technology and creative industries. From October, the universities will add 10 dual-degree programs at undergraduate and postgraduate levels, covering artificial intelligence and data science, computing, business and management, hospitality and tourism, sustainable business, and education. A key focus of the expanded partnership is work-integrated education, with employer-informed projects, capstone modules and applied assessments to give students greater exposure to workplace practices and expectations. The initiatives will draw on BUV's network of more than 500 corporate partners in Vietnam and Manchester Metropolitan's employer relationships in the U.K. and other markets. BUV is also developing an Employability Passport to document students' professional and personal skills, along with their international study and mobility experience. The passport will be awarded alongside degrees at graduation. The universities also plan to introduce semester exchanges and explore summer schools at Manchester Metropolitan's U.K. campus, joint capstone projects, faculty exchanges, jointly developed teaching materials and shared approaches to assessing work-integrated modules. The expanded collaboration will apply work-integrated learning across 15 programs. Supporting graduate employability The partnership aligns with Manchester Metropolitan's Road to 2035 strategy, which emphasizes education and research that prepare graduates for a changing labor market, as well as international partnerships and global engagement. For BUV, the agreement supports its employability strategy, which combines U.K. degree programs in Vietnam with employer partnerships and professional experience. The partnership also comes under the broader U.K.-Vietnam Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, agreed in October 2025, which identifies education and skills as areas of bilateral cooperation. "We are proud of our partnership with Vietnam, and today's signing is another example of our growing collaboration across education and skills," U.K. Minister for Skills Jacqui Smith said. "Through partnerships like this agreement, we are creating new opportunities for learners on opposite sides of the globe and helping equip them with the skills needed for the jobs of the future." Bennett said the partnership would connect academic learning more closely with the needs of an increasingly globalized world. "We aim to co-develop future-ready programs that respond to the demand for highly skilled professionals, while supporting the development of kind, confident, and highly employable graduates who can contribute positively to Vietnam's society and economy," he said. Watling said the collaboration would give students more opportunities to connect their studies with the workplace while strengthening links between the two universities. "By bringing together the strengths of both institutions, we can create more opportunities for students to connect their studies with the world of work while strengthening links between our colleagues and the wider university communities," she said. She noted that Manchester Metropolitan has been named Modern University of the Year for two consecutive years by The Times and Sunday Times Good University Guide and holds a Gold rating under the Teaching Excellence Framework. "We're delighted to be building on two years of collaboration and look forward to seeing how this partnership develops," she said.

picked.t: World Bank lifts Vietnam’s 2026 GDP growth forecast to 7.4%
picked.body: Its latest East Asia and Pacific Economic Update, released on Tuesday, said Vietnam’s growth was expected to remain robust this year before moderating slightly to 7.3% in both 2027 and 2028. The upgrade reflects the stronger performance of the manufacturing and export sectors, particularly the production and shipment of high-tech and artificial intelligence (AI)-related products. The World Bank expects this trend to continue, supported by increased domestic stimulus from structural reforms and expanded public investment. However, inflationary pressures are expected to remain a concern, according to the report. Consumer price inflation in Vietnam is projected to average 4.2% in 2026, driven mainly by higher fuel, housing and utility costs. The upgrade puts Vietnam among the stronger performers in the East Asia and Pacific region, which as a whole is projected to grow 4.5% in 2026. Malaysia and Thailand are forecast to see economic growths of 5.1% and 2%, respectively. AI adoption gathers pace The report highlighted Vietnam’s growing adoption of AI , adding that the regional pace and scale of adoption remain uneven across developing economies. Among emerging-market and developing economies, Malaysia and Vietnam recorded the highest levels of individual generative AI use in early 2026. In Vietnam, AI applications are already being used in a range of practical areas. An AI coach tailored to Vietnamese speakers has become one of the country’s popular language-learning tools, while AI-powered medical imaging is helping under-resourced hospitals improve diagnoses. Small hotels and tour operators are also using AI to generate promotional visuals and apply dynamic pricing at lower cost. The World Bank said these examples illustrate the potential of what it calls "Small AI"—the adoption or adaptation of existing AI tools for specific local needs rather than developing costly frontier models. For most developing economies, adopting and adapting existing technologies is likely to deliver greater benefits in the near term, particularly when tools are tailored to local languages and economic conditions. But the report warned that AI adoption alone would not be enough to deliver broad-based productivity gains. Businesses face constraints including skills shortages, high adoption costs and concerns over security and data privacy. It also noted that demand for AI-related skills in emerging and developing economies in the region remains relatively low compared with other emerging markets, pointing to the need for stronger investment in skills and education. Reliable electricity and sound governance are also important for attracting investment in data centers. Southeast Asian economies could benefit from opportunities in semiconductor manufacturing and other parts of the AI value chain. The World Bank said governments should create an enabling environment for AI adoption by improving digital and energy infrastructure, access to capital and skills, while also using AI themselves to improve public services.

picked.t: HCMC battles flooding as aging infrastructure struggles against intensifying rains, tides
picked.body: Heavy rains from late September to early October caused severe flooding along many roads, disrupting traffic. On the afternoon of Sept. 30, Phan Huy Ich Street in Tan Son Ward was under nearly a meter of water along an 800-meter stretch, according to the Center for Transport and Technical Infrastructure Management. A woman named Phuong Thanh, 33, who lives at Phuc Yen 1 Apartment Building on the street, said it often floods during heavy rains, but never as badly as on that day. "The water reached an adult's waist," said Thanh, who decided to leave her motorbike at a shop and waded home to be safer. According to the Construction Department, Phan Huy Ich Street lies at the intersection of several small drainage basins. Most of the water flows into the Hy Vong Canal before draining into the Tham Luong-Ben Cat Canal, but the aging drain pipes there are too narrow to handle the volume, while the canal has also deteriorated and been encroached upon. It receives runoff from multiple roads, which often overwhelms the drainage system. This problem is not limited to Phan Huy Ich. Ho Chi Minh City now has 159 frequent flooding hotspots, including 76 in the former city, ranging from severe to minor. The rest are in the former Binh Duong and Ba Ria-Vung Tau provinces that were merged into the city last year. Fifty are classified as severely flooded. According to the construction department's review of the city's flood-control program before the redrawing of the provincial borders, HCMC had 126 major roads prone to rain-related flooding and 95 affected by high tides in 2008. But more than 80% of the roads have been fixed since. Improvement works along the Nhieu Loc-Thi Nghe and Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canals have helped resolve flooding in many areas, but some streets like Nguyen Van Khoi, Phan Huy Ich, Le Van Luong, and Tran Xuan Soan remain in bad shape. The city has about 7,200 km of drainage pipes, 1,700 outfalls, more than 500 tidal-control valves, and tidal-control sluices and river embankments. Its nearly 1,000 km of canals and waterways serve as natural drainage routes. Most of this infrastructure is concentrated in the former HCMC, and was developed under two major drainage and flood-control plans, Plans 752 and 1547. One plan focused on developing the drainage network and improving urban canals and waterways, and the other involved building embankments and tidal-control gates. Assoc. Prof. Nguyen Phu Quynh, deputy director of the Southern Institute of Water Resources Research, said that, before 2008, the city largely followed an approach of "fighting floods wherever they occurred," before gradually shifting toward basin-wide flood management. However, delays in completing many projects have limited their effectiveness, with a notable example being the VND10 trillion (US$400 million) flood-control network , which, when completed, is expected to protect around 6.5 million people from flooding with six tidal-control sluice gates. Began in 2016, it has yet to be completed. Dr. Nguyen Huu Nguyen of the Ho Chi Minh City Association for Urban Planning and Development said the drainage system is also under growing pressure from urbanization and changing rainfall and tidal patterns. He said major drainage pipes were previously designed for around 85 mm of rain over three hours and a peak tide of 1.32 m, but in recent years, rainfall in that period has often exceeded 100 mm, while tides at Phu An Station at the Bach Dang Wharf Park have recently reached 1.75 meters on several occasions. On Sept. 30 Phan Huy Ich Street received 79 mm of rain in just 45 minutes, well above the rainfall level it can cope with, it placed further pressure on the aging drainage system and overloaded canals, he said. He said the expanding concrete surfaces have reduced the soil's natural ability to absorb water. Water on the streets must pass through inlets, secondary drains, main drainage pipes, and canals before reaching rivers. Many old and undersized pipes are obstructed by garbage or lack proper connections, preventing water from draining quickly enough. "This explains why areas such as the former Go Vap and Thu Duc districts, despite being on higher ground, still frequently flood." Le Ngoc Linh, deputy director of the construction department, said the differences in terrain and hydrological conditions have made flood control more complex, especially with the impacts of extreme rainfall, high tides, sea-level rise, and land subsidence. The city is currently divided into 23 major drainage basins as the basis for flood management. Flood-control measures must thus consider the entire path of the water flow rather than simply improving the location where flooding occurs. 87 projects completed by 2030 Under a new plan, HCMC expects to complete 87 projects between now and 2030 at a cost of VND142.34 trillion ($5.4 billion), targeting mitigation of 50 severe flooding spots. This year, three locations are expected to be cleared: Phan Van Hon and Binh Quoi

picked.t: HCMC villa basements remain flooded 12 hours after heavy rain
picked.body: Following torrential rain on Wednesday evening, the underground parking garage of a villa in the Cityland Park Hills residential development in Go Vap Ward remained deeply flooded on Thursday morning. Spanning nearly 27 hectares along Phan Van Tri and Nguyen Van Luong streets, the upscale urban complex integrates villas, townhouses, and high-rise apartments with on-site schools, public parks, and retail amenities. Nearly 10 motorbikes of the employees of a Shinhan Bank branch are almost buried under water in the basement parking lot. The deluge also seeped into the building's elevator shaft and electrical control room, inflicting structural and equipment damage. Mud and debris are left amid damaged furniture, medical equipment, and clinical records inside an obstetrics and gynecology clinic after floodwaters were pumped clear. Luong Thi Huong, 60, the clinic's owner, said water rushed into the basement so rapidly the previous evening that staff only managed to push motorbikes out to safety. The surge completely submerged an ultrasound scanner, a urine analyzer, computer terminals, patient files, and multiple television sets. Huong gestures toward a visible high-water mark along the wall, showing floodwaters in the basement reached over a meter deep. "All the clinic's belongings are damaged now. I never expected something like this to happen here," she said. Documents, medicines and medical examination equipment were damaged after being submerged for hours. The downpour on Wednesday evening inundated roadways throughout Ho Chi Minh City, stalling scores of vehicles and triggering widespread traffic gridlock. A persistent atmospheric setup, driven by an active intertropical convergence zone coupled with weak easterly wave disturbances, has triggered sustained, widespread rainfall across Ho Chi Minh City for over 10 days. Meteorological agencies project further precipitation with heavy rainfall across the city through the afternoons and evenings of Oct. 8 and 9. The location of Cityland Park Hills. picked.t: 4 Southeast Asian countries among world's 20 best for travelers this year
picked.body: Indonesia ranked 8th, according to the annual Readers' Choice Awards' survey that asks travelers to rate countries on factors such as culture, attractions, cuisine, and overall experience. "Bali is undoubtedly the touristic hub of the nation, offering everything from holistic jungle retreats to backpacking havens and chic beach clubs. But as the Balinese sense visitor numbers tipping into overtourism territory, the rest of the world’s largest archipelagic country comes into the spotlight," the magazine wrote. Thailand claimed the 10th spot. Thailand's enduring popularity stems from its diverse landscapes and relatively easy transport connections. Travelers can move between destinations by train, domestic flights, boats and overnight buses. From Chiang Mai's lively night markets to the country's picturesque islands, Thailand offers a wide range of experiences. Vietnam ranked 14th on the list. Vietnam welcomed a record 21.2 million international visitors in 2025. Although visitor numbers remain below long-time rival Thailand's, tourism is growing as travelers seek out its diverse landscapes, towns and cultures. Improved air connections have also made previously hard-to-reach destinations more accessible, turning Vietnam from an emerging destination into one firmly on travelers' itineraries, the magazine wrote. Cambodia ranked 16th. Cambodia is best known for Angkor Wat, but its appeal extends far beyond the ancient temple complex. Travelers can explore Phnom Penh's lively markets, the remote Cardamom Mountains and pristine beaches, especially during the dry season from November to April. Greece was ranked the best country in the world for tourists, followed by Japan and Italy. The Readers' Choice Awards, selected by over 800,000 readers, is the longest-running honor in the travel industry that recognizes excellence in hotels, resorts, and destinations worldwide.

picked.t: 하노이시, 상반기 신규아파트 중 고급부문 비중 78% 달해…서민형 사실상 ‘실종’
picked.body: 기사 이해를 돕기위해 AI를 활용해 제작한 이미지입니다. 올 들어 베트남 수도 하노이에 새로 공급된 아파트 10채 중 8채가 ㎡당 5,000만 동(1,924달러) 이상인 고급 아파트인 것으로 나타났다. 실제 수요가 가장 높은 서민형 아파트는 사실상 시장에서 자취를 감춘 모양새다. 하노이시 인민의회 도시위원회가 최근 내놓은 보고서에 따르면, 올해 상반기 6개월간 하노이시 전체 주택 공급 가운데 상업용 아파트의 비중은 70%에 달했다. 같은 기간 전체 거래량 중 73%는 아파트가 차지했다. 특히 신규 분양된 상업용 아파트 가운데 78%는 분양가가 ㎡당 5,000만~8,000만 동(1,924~3,079달러)인 고급 아파트와 8,000만 동/㎡ 이상의 하이엔드 아파트가 차지한 반면, ㎡당 2,500만 동 미만 서민형 아파트는 시장에서 거의 찾아볼 수 없었다. 도시위원회는 아파트 전체 공급량과 부문별 공급량에 대해서는 정확한 수치를 공개하지 않았지만, 주거 공급 구조에서 수급 불균형이 심화하고 있는 모습이 확인된 것이다. 글로벌 부동산 컨설팅 업체 CBRE에 따르면, 상반기 하노이에 신규 공급된 아파트 수는 모두 1만6,600호로 2020년 이후 상반기 최고치를 기록했다. 그러나 ㎡당 분양가가 6,000만 동(2,309달러) 미만인 아파트가 2개 분기 연속 공급되지 않는 등 상품 구조에도 뚜렷한 변화가 나타났다. CBRE에 따르면 2분기 말 기준 아파트 신규 분양가는 평균 ㎡당 약 9,500만 동(3,656달러, 부가세·유지보수비·할인액 제외)에 이른 것으로 집계됐다. 이는 전분기보다 12%, 지난해 같은 기간보다 21% 각각 높은 수준이다. 베트남부동산중개인협회(VARs) 역시 2분기 하노이에서 신규 분양된 주거 사업 대부분이 고급·하이엔드 상품인 것으로 추정했다. 협회에 따르면, 현재 하노이 도심지 아파트 평균 분양가는 ㎡당 1억2,100만 동(4,657달러)에 달한다. 도시위원회는 “지난 2년간 시장은 단기 가격 상승 기대와 포모(FOMO)에 이끌려 가격이 급등하며 과열되는 양상을 보였다면, 올 들어 지금까지 베트남 부동산 시장은 2024~2025년과 엇갈리는 흐름을 보이고 있다”고 평가했다. 도시위원회 보고서에 따르면, 올해 부동산 시장은 낮은 유동성과 거래로 인해 침체된 양상을 보이고 있으며, 거래는 주로 사회주택이나 서민형 주택 등 저가형 주택에 집중되는 모습을 보이고 있다. 도시위원회는 "개발 소문을 보고 사들인 투기성 택지나 적절한 커뮤니티 시설이 형성되지 않은 프로젝트는 가격이 크게 내렸음에도 거래가 좀처럼 이뤄지지 않고 있다"고 밝혔다. 상업용 주택과는 대조적으로 집값이 상대적으로 저렴한 사회주택은 긍정적인 변화를 보이고 있다. 올 들어 하노이에서 착공된 사회주택 사업은 총 33건, 3만 세대 규모로 정부가 부여한 목표를 초과 달성했다. 이어 내년에는 27개 사업을 통해 2만8,696세대 규모의 사회주택이 공급될 예정이며, 2028~2030년 기간 101개 사업, 8만6,216세대의 추가 공급이 예정돼 있다.

picked.t: A love story across continents ends in a packed Vietnamese village wedding
picked.body: By the middle of the banquet in O Dien Commune in early September, the village cultural house was packed and sweltering. Guests from Ireland, Australia, Switzerland and Brazil searched for seats as the usual six-person table arrangement quickly fell apart. Five translators moved between tables, arranging extra chairs, bringing ice and drinks, and at times showing foreign guests how to use chopsticks. Thao, a preschool teacher, had initially expected only 35 to 38 overseas guests. But after sending out invitations she had designed herself eight months earlier, interest in experiencing a traditional Vietnamese wedding spread among her friends. The final count reached 65, forcing her family to add two tables at the last minute. Initially, Thao, a preschool teacher, only expected to get 35 to 38 foreign guests. However, after she mailed her self-designed invitations eight months earlier, word had been getting around. Excitement about a fully traditional Vietnamese wedding spread through conversations among Thao’s friends, and the final headcount surged to 65. The wedding Thao had meticulously planned suddenly turned into a scramble, and her family had to set up two extra tables at the last minute. Standing in the corner of the cultural house, seeing her husband Eoin Aylward, from Kilkenny, Ireland, and his family looking radiant in the traditional Vietnamese ao dai , she realized her worry had been unnecessary. They had traveled more than 10,000 kilometers just to witness this moment. That journey began with a chance encounter four years ago in Australia. In 2022, she had left Hanoi for Australia with the intention of living there for a year or two before returning home. She worked at a coffee shop near where Aylward lived. Her first impression of the Irish civil engineer wasn't great: he was quiet and always looked tense because of work pressure. However, he quietly won over the Vietnamese woman. During the freezing Australian winter, he persistently woke up at 5 a.m. to drive her to work and pick her up afterward. When Thao decided to study to rebuild her career as a preschool teacher, he became her greatest source of emotional support. "Every time I doubted myself, Eoin would hold my hand and say, 'You can definitely do it,'" Thao recalls. "Our love was not built on magic, but from car rides at 5 a.m." In the summer of 2025, he took Thao to a bridge associated with wish-making tales in Ireland, and handed her a traditional Claddagh ring, an Irish cultural symbol featuring two hands clasping a crowned heart, representing unity, love, and loyalty. After he proposed, she expressed the wish to host a proper Vietnamese wedding in her hometown, to which he immediately agreed. The couple had to make many compromises to arrive at the wedding date they wanted. He had originally hoped for a church wedding, but a traditional Vietnamese wedding already runs long, with a series of customs to observe. She then patiently showed him videos of Vietnamese weddings, and carefully explained the spiritual significance of ancestral rites. Once he understood that these were not superficial formalities but a connection to her roots, he enthusiastically explained them to his parents and friends. On the big day, the groom's family prepared seven elaborate betrothal trays. The groomsmen, all tall foreigners dressed in colorful ao dai, walked through the winding and narrow alleys of O Dien. Villagers poured out to watch, taking pictures with their phones, and the laughter and chatter chased away the smothering heat. Relatives and friends of Aylward from Ireland, Australia, Switzerland, Brazil, and elsewhere were excited about Vietnamese wedding rituals. That day, fried chicken from KFC also made a special appearance alongside traditional boiled chicken with lime leaves at the 140-table banquet, because Thao was worried that the foreign guests might not find the local food to their liking. In the end, everyone was keen to try a Vietnamese village feast, with a guest "eating three large pieces of chicken." Neighborhood grandmas and mothers, delighted to have them, kept smiling. When Thao stood on stage to thank her parents, many Irish guests were in tears. "They told me they were moved by the closeness and bond of the Vietnamese people. At that moment, language and geographical boundaries vanished," Thao says. Amidst the bustle atmosphere, Aylward looked at Thao and whispered softly, "We did it."
